newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechens urge Russia to complete troop withdrawal.
newsitem.headline: Chechens urge Russia to complete troop withdrawal.

text.p: Chechen separatist leaders increased their pressure on Moscow to withdraw remaining Russian forces from the rebel province before local polls due in January, Interfax news agency said on Monday.

Interfax quoted the head of the Chechen parliament as saying the presence of two Russian brigades could destabilise the voting in which the population of the conflict-torn region is expected to elect a new leader and a new legislature.
"They (the troops) are the most destabilising factor in the republic," said Akhyad Idigov.
"The so-called "third force' can use their presence any time to stage military provocations," he said, referring to mysterious forces blamed by both sides for undermining peace efforts.
Russia, which sent in troops in December 1994 to quell Chechnya's independence bid, pulled out most of them under the latest peace deal without reaching most of its aims.

The rebels agreed in the agreement struck on August 31 to put off for five years a formal decision on the region's future political status but made little secret of the fact that they still want their mountainous homeland to be fully independent.
Moscow rules out granting full independence to Chechnya and says it wants to keep troops in the region as a sign of its presence there.

Interfax quoted Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov as saying on Monday that Moscow want to keep in Chechnya up to 5,000 troops reporting to him and the same number reporting to the Defence Ministry. He also said up to 800 Russian police should stay in Chechnya.
Kulikov said that up to 20,000 Russian troops and some 2,500 police were currently stationed in the region.

Despite Moscow's military presence in Chechnya the rebels have regained control over most of the region. They have appointed their government and scheduled a regional election for January 27, dealing the Kremlin a fait accompli which it has reluctantly been forced to accept.

On Sunday the former pro-Moscow leader of Chechnya, Doku Zavgayev, formally dissolved his government which had been sheltering for several months inside the Russian military base at Severny airport outside the regional capital Grozny.

Interfax said on Monday Russian officials sealed the offices of Zavgayev's ministers, most of whom had already been evacuated either to Russia or to northern Chechnya, over which Moscow still maintains partial control.

The rebels and President Boris Yeltsin's envoy to Chechnya Ivan Rybkin announced after talks held last week that they were close to striking another deal which would clarify their relations until the local polls.

No details of the agreement, which is due to be signed by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Chechen government head Aslan Maskhadov, have been released so far. Rybkin and Chernomyrdin met to discuss the agreement on Monday.
The deal is intended to allow Russia to start investing in the post-war reconstruction of Chechnya.
The rebels have been seeking compensation from Moscow for the wholesale destruction in their republic caused by the conflict.
Moscow wants to use funds to ensure that the region remains part of the Russian Federation.
